patients.summary: Healthy corporate project manager who joins in 2023. From early 2025 she has intermittent dysphagia and chest discomfort that fail a PPI trial; ENT calls it esophageal dysmotility, a barium swallow shows corkscrew contractions, EGD is normal and manometry in 2026 shows distal esophageal spasm managed without medication.

documents.title: Office Visit - Chest discomfort / dysphagia
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: 44F, about 10 days of intermittent episodes where food or a drink feels like it stops behind the sternum, sometimes with a tight discomfort in the same spot. Happens with solids and with liquids. Comes and goes on its own. Not exertional. No dyspnea, palpitations, diaphoresis. Denies weight loss, vomiting up undigested food, pain with swallowing, or any long-standing heartburn. No new meds. Work has been heavy this month.

PMH none. Meds none. NKDA. Never smoker. FH: father HTN, mother hypothyroid; no premature CAD she knows of.

O: vitals normal. Comfortable. Oropharynx clear, neck without mass or nodes, thyroid normal. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Chest wall nontender. Abdomen soft, no epigastric tenderness. No edema.
ECG in office: sinus rhythm, normal intervals, no ST-T changes.

A/P: Intermittent dysphagia to solids and liquids with retrosternal discomfort. Not anginal by history, ECG normal. Most likely reflux-related - trial of omeprazole 20 mg each morning before breakfast. Let me know in 3-4 weeks if not better; if no response, will get her to a specialist for a swallowing workup. Go to the ED for chest pain that is constant, exertional, or with shortness of breath, or if food truly will not pass.

documents.title: Referral to Otolaryngology
documents.author: PCP

documents.title: Otolaryngology Consultation
documents.author: otolaryngology
documents.body:
Outside otolaryngology group - consultation letter
Date of visit: 02/28/2025
Re: Abigail Paquette, DOB 07/27/1980

Thank you for asking us to see Ms. Paquette, a 44-year-old project manager, for six weeks of swallowing trouble and chest discomfort.

She describes episodes in which a bite, or a sip, lodges at about the level of the mid-sternum. Some episodes bring a sharp, squeezing pain there that can travel through to her back. They last anywhere from a few minutes up to an hour, happen several times a week and usually pass without her doing anything. Very hot or very cold drinks can set them off, and she suspects pressure at work sometimes does as well. A course of omeprazole made no difference.

She has no meaningful past medical history and takes nothing regularly. Drug allergies: none known. No food allergy, no asthma. Family history notable for maternal hypothyroidism and paternal hypertension. She has never smoked and drinks one or two drinks a week.

Review of systems: no weight loss, no vomiting of undigested food, no odynophagia, no chronic heartburn.

Examination: vital signs stable. Well appearing. No pallor or other sign of anemia. Ears, nose and oral cavity normal. Oropharynx and neck without mass; no cervical lymphadenopathy; thyroid unremarkable. Heart and lung sounds normal.

Her ECG from your office on 01/27/2025, which I reviewed, is unremarkable.

Impression: The pattern - dysphagia to liquids as well as solids, a mid-chest level, thermal triggers, chest pain and no response to acid suppression - points to an esophageal motility disorder rather than an oropharyngeal or structural problem. I have recorded this as esophageal dysmotility.

Recommendations:
1. Gastroenterology evaluation for esophageal workup.
2. In the meantime, avoid very hot or very cold beverages and take smaller bites.
3. No ENT follow-up needed unless new throat or voice symptoms.

Thank you for involving our service.
Otolaryngology

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual. Also the swallowing problem is back.

Interval: the episodes from the winter faded out by April and she was fine over the summer. Starting about three weeks ago they returned - food and liquids hanging up mid-chest, and now some bringing back of undigested food after meals, which she did not have before. Occasional pressure-like pain behind the breastbone during episodes. Worse on high-stress days at work. Weight stable by our scale. No vomiting, no black stools or blood. No heartburn.

Meds: none. NKDA. Problem list: esophageal dysmotility (ENT impression 2/2025).
Social and family history unchanged.

ROS otherwise negative.

Exam: well. Vitals normal. HEENT benign, no cervical nodes, thyroid normal. Heart regular without murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organomegaly. No edema. Skin unremarkable.

A/P:
1. Esophageal dysmotility, symptoms recurrent with new regurgitation. Barium swallow ordered and GI referral placed again - she is ready to go this time. Same precautions: if food impacts and won't pass, ED.
2. Health maintenance: turned 45 this summer - discussed colon screening options, she prefers FIT; kit given. Mammogram order placed. Pap/HPV due next year. Labs: CBC, CMP, lipids, TSH. Flu vaccine today. PHQ-2 0.
RTC 1 yr, sooner as needed.

reports.text:
Indication: dysphagia to solids and liquids. Technique: single- and double-contrast esophagram with thin barium, followed by a barium tablet.
Oropharyngeal phase: normal bolus transit, no laryngeal penetration or aspiration.
Esophagus: on several swallows the distal esophagus shows intermittent non-propulsive contractions producing a corkscrew appearance, between which primary peristalsis is normal. The esophagus is not dilated. No stricture, ring, web, mass or diverticulum. Mucosa smooth. The barium tablet passed into the stomach without delay.
Gastroesophageal junction opens normally. No hiatal hernia. No reflux observed during the exam.
reports.conclusion: Intermittent corkscrew-like esophageal contractions, suggestive of a spastic motility disorder. No structural abnormality.

reports.text:
Specimen A: esophagus, distal, biopsies. Specimen B: esophagus, proximal/mid, biopsies.
Gross: A and B - multiple tan soft tissue fragments.
Microscopic: squamous mucosa with normal maturation. No increase in intraepithelial eosinophils. No basal cell hyperplasia, no intestinal metaplasia, no dysplasia. No fungal organisms.
reports.conclusion: A and B: benign squamous mucosa. No increased intraepithelial eosinophils. Negative for dysplasia.

documents.title: Upper Endoscopy Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside gastroenterology - endoscopy unit
Procedure date: 02/10/2026
Patient: Abigail Paquette, DOB 07/27/1980
Procedure: esophagogastroduodenoscopy with cold forceps biopsy
Indication: dysphagia to solids and liquids; esophagram with corkscrew contractions.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care, propofol per anesthesia record.
Allergies: NKDA.

Findings:
- Esophagus: normal caliber and mucosa throughout. No rings, furrows, exudate, stricture or mass. Z-line regular. Biopsies taken from the distal and the proximal/mid esophagus to exclude eosinophilic esophagitis.
- Stomach: normal mucosa; retroflexion normal, no hiatal hernia.
- Duodenum: normal through the second portion.
The scope traversed the GE junction without resistance.

Impression: normal upper endoscopy; no structural cause for dysphagia. Pathology pending.
Recommendations: follow up in GI clinic 03/03/2026 as scheduled. Resume regular diet today.
No complications. Discharged home with an escort.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Clinic Note
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside gastroenterology group
Visit date: 03/03/2026
Patient: Abigail Paquette, 45 y/o F
Referring: primary care physician

Reason for visit: return visit after EGD; dysphagia.

HPI: Ms. Paquette comes back to clinic roughly a year after ENT first saw her for this. Over the past six months she has had on-and-off trouble getting both solids and liquids down, episodes of undigested food coming back up, and now and then pain behind the sternum. She ties many episodes to emotionally stressful stretches at work. No weight loss, no vomiting, no hematemesis or melena.

Problem list: esophageal dysmotility.
Medications: none.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: hypothyroidism in her mother, hypertension in her father.
Social: never smoker, 1-2 alcoholic drinks weekly, works as a corporate project manager.

Exam: normal. Well appearing, abdomen soft and nontender, no lymphadenopathy.

Data reviewed:
- Barium esophagram 10/07/2025: intermittent corkscrew-type contractions of the esophagus, no structural lesion.
- EGD 02/10/2026: no structural abnormality. Biopsies benign without eosinophilia.

Assessment: esophageal dysmotility. The corkscrew pattern with a structurally normal esophagus most suggests a spastic disorder such as distal esophageal spasm; achalasia needs to be excluded before treatment is chosen.

Plan:
1. High-resolution esophageal manometry - ordered.
2. Avoid very hot and very cold drinks, eat slowly with smaller bites, stay upright for a while after meals.
3. No medication for now; will decide after manometry.
4. Telehealth follow-up after the study.

Gastroenterology

reports.text: Solid-state high-resolution manometry, Chicago Classification v4.0 protocol. Upper esophageal sphincter: normal resting pressure and relaxation. EGJ: median IRP 9 mmHg (normal). Esophageal body, 10 supine wet swallows: 4 premature (distal latency under 4.5 s), 6 normal peristalsis; no failed or hypercontractile swallows. Upright and multiple rapid swallows concordant.
reports.conclusion: Distal esophageal spasm (Chicago Classification v4.0). Normal EGJ relaxation; no achalasia.

documents.title: High-Resolution Esophageal Manometry
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside gastroenterology - motility laboratory
Study date: 04/08/2026
Patient: Abigail Paquette, DOB 07/27/1980
Indication: dysphagia; esophagram with corkscrew contractions; normal EGD.

Protocol: solid-state high-resolution catheter placed transnasally without difficulty. Supine 10 water swallows, followed by upright swallows and multiple rapid swallows per Chicago Classification v4.0. Patient tolerated well.

Upper esophageal sphincter: normal resting pressure and relaxation.
Esophagogastric junction: median integrated relaxation pressure 9 mmHg (normal).
Esophageal body (supine): 10 wet swallows evaluated. 4 of 10 premature (distal latency less than 4.5 seconds). The remaining 6 showed normal peristalsis. No failed and no hypercontractile swallows.
Upright and provocative maneuvers: consistent with the supine findings.

Interpretation: normal EGJ relaxation with premature contractions in 40% of swallows. Meets criteria for distal esophageal spasm (Chicago Classification v4.0). No evidence of achalasia.

Motility laboratory, gastroenterology

documents.title: Gastroenterology Telehealth Follow-up
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside gastroenterology group - video visit 04/21/2026
Patient: Abigail Paquette

Reviewed her manometry with her: normal sphincter relaxation and premature contractions on 4 of 10 swallows, which classifies her esophageal dysmotility as distal esophageal spasm. Achalasia excluded. This matches the corkscrew esophagram and her symptom triggers.

We talked through management. Episodes remain intermittent. Because they are intermittent and she does well between them, she would like to keep to the measures already in place rather than start a medication. Reasonable. If episodes become more frequent or harder to tolerate, a trial of a calcium channel blocker is the next step, and we would revisit other options after that.

Plan: continue avoiding temperature extremes in drinks, small bites, eating slowly, upright after meals. No medications started. Return to GI clinic in about six months, sooner as needed. Medications: none. Allergies: NKDA.

Gastroenterology
